newsitem.title: UK: UK's IMRO takes trusts to task on unquoted stocks.
newsitem.headline: UK's IMRO takes trusts to task on unquoted stocks.

text.p: Britain's Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO) said on Wednesday it was continuing a review of the unit trust industry by looking at 100 trusts where it had identified holdings of unquoted securities.

The review was sparked by IMRO's investigation into irregularities in two unit trusts and an investment fund run by Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM), part of the Deutsche Bank AG banking empire.
An IMRO spokesman told Reuters the so-called "themed visits" were following up last week's review, which showed that only 13 percent of trusts held unquoted securities.

The visits, which had not all been completed, were concentrating on how a firm had structured itself, with particular emphasis on how valuations of unquoted stocks were undertaken, the spokesman said.

A cross-section of trusts would be examined and the results then pooled. IMRO aimed to find out how firms get valuations, how frequently they are updated, who signs them off and other questions such as what role a trustee had in confirming them.
If any breaches of IMRO rules were identified during the course of this, they would be rectified, he added.
With reference to the MGAM probe itself, the spokesman confirmed reports that IMRO had replaced accountancy firm Deloitte Touche because a conflict of interest had emerged.

He said Arthur Andersen had now taken on the investigation alongside IMRO investigators, with the aim of discovering what compensation, if any, was due to investors in the three MGAM funds, which were temporarily suspended two weeks ago.
"I can confirm that Arthur Andersen has been appointed. They have been fully briefed and have commenced work on several fronts," he said.

He denied reports that the IMRO investigation had stalled because of the discovery, adding the watchdog had been fact-finding and collating information since day one and this process would now carry on in conjunction with Arthur Andersen.
"There's no question that any time has been wasted here," IMRO's Andrew Beagley told Reuters.
